plan.topic_summary: Backside power delivery (BSPDN) is a semiconductor manufacturing technique that moves power routing to the backside of the silicon die, freeing frontside area for transistors and interconnect. It matters for a 1–5 year view because it is a prerequisite for continued scaling at leading-edge process nodes and will reshape foundry roadmaps, equipment demand, and packaging architectures.
key_questions: Which foundries have BSPDN in high-volume production as of the next 12 months, and at what reported yield or defect-density levels?
How does BSPDN affect total cost of ownership per wafer at 3 nm and below compared to frontside-only power delivery, and what is the breakeven point for adoption?
What new or modified equipment (lithography, etch, deposition, metrology) is required for BSPDN, and how concentrated is the supplier base?
How does BSPDN interact with advanced packaging (chiplet, 2.5 D, 3 D stacking) over the next 3–5 years, and does it enable or constrain those architectures?
What are the known or projected reliability and thermal limitations of backside power networks under sustained high-power workloads, and how do they compare to frontside baselines?

gaps: No quantitative yield or cost-overhead data for BSPDN in high-volume manufacturing; Intel 10-K confirms HVM but provides no yield figures, and R5 explicitly flags absence of BPDN-specific reliability quantification.

sources.title: Intel PowerVia Technology: Backside Power Delivery for High Density and High-Performance Computing
sources.venue: IEEE Symposium on VLSI Technology and Circuits (VLSI Technology and Circuits)
sources.abstract: This paper presents a high-yielding backside power delivery (BPD) technology, PowerVia, implemented on Intel 4 finFET process. PowerVia more directly integrates power delivery to the transistor as compared to published buried power rail schemes, enabling additional wiring resources on front side for signal routing. A fabricated E-core with $\gt 90$% cell utilization showed $\gt 30$% platform voltage droop improvement and 6% frequency benefit compared to a similar design without PowerVia. Transistor performance, reliability, and fault isolation capability is detailed.

sources.title: CSCO: A Backside-PDN-Aware Clock-Signal Co-Optimization Framework for Improved PPA
sources.abstract: Backside power delivery networks (BSPDN) have emerged as a promising technology for advanced logic nodes to address IR-drop and PPA challenges. While BSPDN introduces additional routing resources on the backside, these resources are limited and must be carefully partitioned between clock and signal nets, creating a critical resource allocation tradeoff. Prior work either moves only the clock network or assumes a fixed clock tree and optimizes only signal nets, failing to explore the tradeoff space of backside resource allocation. Moreover, lacking frontside power-ground shielding, BSPDN introduces severe signal integrity (SI) degradation. We propose CSCO, a data-driven BSPDN-aware co-optimization framework that jointly allocates limited backside resources between clock and signal nets across frontside/backside layers. CSCO employs efficient search strategies to identify critical nets for backside routing without repeated evaluation, navigating the clock-signal allocation tradeoff to balance IR-drop, routing congestion, and PPA. The framework also leverages backside routing to mitigate coupling noise and crosstalk-induced SI issues. Experiments demonstrate improved WNS/TNS, frequency, and SI robustness without additional shielding overhead.

sources.title: Leading Edge Technologies: Backside Power Delivery
sources.abstract: Abstract An architectural shift to buried power rails (BPRs) with backside power delivery (BPD) is on the horizon as CMOS technology approaches the 2 nm node. The obstruction created by the presence of BPD networks obsoletes many of the electrical fault isolation (EFI) techniques that have been used for the past few decades and severely degrades the performance of others. This chapter provides an overview of EFI methods that are still applicable to ICs with BPD networks, including e-beam and atomic force probing, x-ray and magnetic field imaging, and lock-in thermography. It assesses the technical challenges of each method as well as the potential for improvement.

sources.title: Design Space Exploration of Backside Clock Meshes for 2 nm GAAFET BSPDN Technology
sources.abstract: Clock meshes are used in high-performance VLSI designs to minimize skew and tolerate on-chip variation, but they spend scarce routing resources on premium metal layers. Backside power delivery creates a new option: it adds thick, low-resistance metal layers on the back of the wafer, and the power grid does not consume all of them. Flip-flops remain on the frontside; a backside mesh therefore cannot drive them directly, and every connection passes through a through-silicon via. We present the first design-space exploration of backside clock meshes, implemented in OpenROAD on GT2N, a 2 nm nanosheet technology. Four benchmarks (1,938 to 15,311 flip-flops) are explored with multi-objective Bayesian optimization, and every design point is verified by transistor-level SPICE simulation, since the cyclic mesh cannot be evaluated by static timing analysis. Across all four designs, the backside mesh consistently outperforms an identical frontside mesh, with on average 45% lower skew, 25% lower sink slew, 4.5% lower power, and 28% less frontside clock wiring, and its skew spread under 10,000-sample Monte Carlo is a third of the frontside mesh's.

sources.title: Transient Multiscale Workflow for Thermal Analysis of 3DHI Chip Stack
sources.abstract: Modern package designs make use of technologies such as backside power delivery (BSPD) and 3D stacked chiplets that require accounting for the heterogeneity in back end of the line (BEOL) structures in hot-spot prediction. Multiscale homogenization strategies have been demonstrated to be effective for steady-state simulations, however accurate 3D transient simulations that include BEOL structures remain an open challenge. In this work, we demonstrate a transient thermal workflow that accounts for the 3D heterogeneous structures in the BEOL for problems with strong- and weak- temporal scale separation under the assumption of temperature independent constitutive properties. Our workflow, based on Bloomfield et. al. 2025, automatically extracts, meshes, and homogenizes thermal properties from GDSII and OASIS files to construct thermal property maps. Property maps (heat capacity and conductivity) have been generated for a 1 mm by 1 mm SoC-style model die that was constructed with LibreLane for 100 by 100 grids with 5 micron by 5 micron representative volume elements (RVEs), and 50 by 50 grids with 10 micron by 10 micron RVEs. The expressions for a transient effective conductivity are provided and a demonstration of the impact of the transient effects are provided for a single RVE. Finally, transient conductivity maps have been provided for a time integration timestep of dt=0.001.

sources.title: Thermal Impacts of Backside Power Delivery Networks on GAAFET Technology
sources.abstract: The emerging backside power delivery network (BSPDN) technology offers significant advantages in area scaling, IR drop reduction, and operating frequency enhancement. In this work, we systematically investigate the thermal dissipation mechanisms associated with various BSPDN architectures and develop SPICE-compatible dynamic thermal models to facilitate model-driven evaluation for electrical and thermal dynamics at the device-circuit level. A comprehensive evaluation, coupled with the previously developed parasitic model, reveals that the parasitic effects dominate circuit dynamic performance compared to self-heating effects (SHEs), while the SHE exacerbates device degradation mechanisms, such as hot carrier injection (HCI) and bias temperature instability (BTI). Evaluation results indicate that backside contacts (BSCs) are more capable of suppressing SHEs and parasitic effects, while through silicon via in middle-of-line (MOL) (TSVM)-based circuits experience pronounced performance degradation, enabling a model-driven tradeoff strategy for circuit optimization in advanced technology.

sources.title: Low Distortion Fusion Bonding using Pneumatically Warped Wafers
sources.venue: 2026 IEEE 76th Electronic Components and Technology Conference (ECTC), Orlando, FL, USA, 2026, pp. 1349-1356
sources.abstract: Backside power-delivery-network (BSPDN) schemes require wafer-to-wafer bonding steps that do not leave high order shape changes or localized stresses in the bonded stack to ensure that these don't get transferred to the thinned wafer for further lithographic exposure. However, bonding mechanics involve strong adhesive forces which can inherently create localized distortions that lithography tools must eventually compensate. Some contributors to grid distortion of the target wafer are, method of bond initiation, bond front velocity variations, and lack of symmetry between the wafers. In this work, we evaluate a low-distortion bonding approach in the SUSS XBA tool, where some of these contributors are tackled at the source, namely by initiating the bond without a localized external force, and keeping the wafers compliant & symmetric during bonding. Wafers are bonded with a slight pre-stress due to controlled gas pressure applied over the whole backside of the wafers throughout bonding. Wafer-shape measurements of the bonded stacks are used to perform gradient-based in-plane-displacements (IPD) modelling to estimate bonding-induced grid distortion. Dense scanner metrology is used on patterned-bonded wafers to confirm the location and severity of distortion predictions from patterned wafer geometry (PWG) measurements. On the PWG distortion maps and scanner grid readouts, we perform alignment and CPE modelling with different field layouts. Sub-10 nm levels of residual grid distortion are achievable with relatively low-order correction models, and less than or equal to 3 nm by using advanced CPE models. These results demonstrate that pneumatically warped bonding yields low-distortion bonded stacks, and that simple process tuning can decouple the dominant distortion source from edge-related variability.

sources.title: Nano-Through Silicon Vias (nTSV) for Backside Power Delivery Networks (BSPDN)
sources.venue: IEEE Symposium on VLSI Technology and Circuits (VLSI Technology and Circuits)
sources.abstract: In this paper we discuss the driving forces for moving to chip backside power delivery. Possible integration flows and challenges are discussed for integrating through-silicon via (TSV) connections that directly interconnect the chip at the standard-cell level. These approaches use power rail integration schemes that can be “buried” in the STI and Si below the devices or directly integrated as backside metallization scheme on the wafer backside. Both nTSV “last” and “first” integration flows have been demonstrated. Key technology challenges are the extreme wafer thinning required and back-side lithography correction to correct for wafer distortions caused by wafer processing and W2W bonding.

sources.title: Thermal Implications of Non-Uniform Power in BSPDN-Enabled 2.5D/3D Chiplet-based Systems-in-Package using Nanosheet Technology
sources.abstract: Advances in nanosheet technologies have significantly increased power densities, exacerbating thermal management challenges in 2.5D/3D chiplet-based Systems-in-Package (SiP). While traditional thermal analyses often employ uniform power maps to simplify computational complexity, this practice neglects localized heating effects, leading to inaccuracies in thermal estimations, especially when comparing power delivery networks (PDN) in 3D integration. This work examines the thermal impact of non-uniform power distributions on SiPs utilizing frontside (FSPDN) and backside (BSPDN) power delivery approaches. Using high-resolution thermal simulations with non-uniform power maps at resolutions down to 5 micrometers, we demonstrate that uniform power assumptions substantially underestimate peak temperatures and fail to reveal critical thermal differences between BSPDN and FSPDN configurations in 3D scenarios. Our results highlight that BSPDN configurations in 3D, although beneficial in simplified uniform scenarios, exhibit pronounced thermal penalties under realistic, localized workloads due to limited lateral heat spreading. These findings emphasize the necessity of adopting fine-grained, workload-aware power maps in early-stage thermal modeling to enable accurate PDN assessment and informed thermal-aware design decisions in advanced nanosheet-based 3D SiP.

sources.title: Thermal Mitigation Strategy for Backside Power Delivery Network
sources.venue: IEEE Electronic Components and Technology Conference (ECTC)
sources.abstract: By improving power delivery capability and mitigating signal routing congestion, Back Side Power Delivery Network (BSPDN) has been proven to be a game changer for the next generation of chip design. However, it also brings thermal challenges due to a significantly larger thermal resistance between the CPU power grid and on-chip forced cooling. Therefore, a cutting-edge cooling scheme is needed to tackle this issue. Inspired by the similarity between Back End of Line (BEOL) layer structure and 3D manifolded microchannel cooler, we propose an innovative embedded microchannel cooling configuration to bring the coolant closer to FEOL, which also cooperates with chip-top jet cooling to form a dual-sided cooling system. Finite Element Analysis (FEA) is performed to study the thermal performance of chips and cooling effectiveness and efficiency for microchannel cooling. Due to the high complexity of a detailed BSPDN model, several engineering approaches are utilized to reduce the computing resource requirement. Detailed Back End of Line (BEOL) thermal models are established and investigated for computing its accurate orthotropic thermal conductivity. Then, a local unit cell model including both BSPDN chip and coolant region are simulated through system coupling approach, after which the effective Heat Transfer Coefficients (HTC) are extracted and applied to a 50 μm × 50 μm overall model with power map heat source. A control parameter study is conducted by varying coolant type of water and air, inlet flow velocity, and inlet flow temperature. It turns out that the microchannel cooling with 283K, 0.06m/s water inlet can reduce the maximum temperature by more than 20% or about 20°C for both uniform heat flux and heat map cases, at an expense of 2581 Pa inlet pressure.

sources.title: Modeling of Backside Power Delivery and Thermal Management in Semiconductor Die Packages
sources.venue: I-THERM :/I-THERM - Intersociety Conference on Thermal Phenomena in Electronic Systems
sources.abstract: Modern semiconductor packaging faces the dual challenges of efficiently delivering power to numerous transistors and managing heat to prevent hotspots and potential component failure. Backside power delivery (BSPD) distinguishes itself from conventional power delivery methods by delivering power from the backside of the silicon die, using unused space for thicker power lines and thereby reducing resistance loss. Embedded microfluidic cooling strategies have investigated microchannels in the back side of silicon dies to direct coolant over hotspots, effectively dissipating heat for chip temperature management. We propose a synergistic integration of microfluidic channels with power delivery on the backside of semiconductor dies that can potentially offer optimized space utilization to allow balanced power and thermal performance. However, this requires modeling tools that can accurately capture coupled electrical and thermal responses in 3D while resolving the small feature sizes relative to the overall die size that can lead to computational complexity. To address this challenge, we develop a model that employs a homogenization method that allows for sub-grid resolution of microscale features, as well as the transformation of the fully 3D problem into an equivalent set of connected 2D subproblem. This work demonstrates application of this method to numerically study a silicon die with both a backside power delivery network (BSPDN) and manifold liquid cooling microchannels. 3D transport is represented by considering the energy and mass exchange between multiple 2D layers. The homogenized representation treats the domain as a porous composite material with metallic power lines navigating between the flow channels. Homogenized conservation thermofluidic conservation equations for the porous medium that consider electrical Joule heating are used to construct the numerical model. Representative steady-state cases are studied where the silicon die generates uniform heating with local hotspots. Through these case studies, we reveal the potential application advantages of integrating 3D manifold microchannels for cooling in a BSPDN for high-power operations.

sources.title: Investigation of bottom-up electrodeposition filling for nanoscale through-silicon vias (TSVs)
Inkjet-printed electrical interconnects for high resolution integrated circuit diagnostics
sources.abstract: Abstract As semiconductors continue to shrink in size and become more three-dimensional in shape, the size of defects that can induce a failure also reduces, pushing the need for better fault isolation. The resolving capability of microscopes used in failure analysis (FA) is frequently limited by how close the microscope can be brought to the circuit under test. Accessibility is often restricted by the presence of probe needles or wire bonds that are needed to power up the device during the measurement. Here, I describe a robust, rapid and cost-effective method to overcome the contacting bottleneck by re-routing the probe pads with a low-profile redistribution layer, realized by conductive inkjet printing. I demonstrate that the method enables analytical FA with high spatial resolution on a backside power delivery network structure in combination with the optical beam induced resistance change (OBIRCH) technique. Electrical and structural characterization of the printing process are also reported.

sources.title: Controllable and Nanoscale Linear Etching of Atomic Layer Deposited Molybdenum Using Cyclic Stepwise CHF 3 /O 2 Plasma
sources.abstract: ABSTRACT Precise nanoscale control of molybdenum (Mo) etching is critical for state‐of‐the‐art interconnects, 3D NAND, and other key applications like back‐side power delivery network. Herein, we demonstrate a controllable, nanoscale etching process for Mo films using a cyclic stepwise CHF 3 /O 2 plasma approach. Compared to continuous etching, cyclic stepwise etching achieves exceptional etching linearity (R 2 = 0.999) with a precisely tunable etch depth per cycle ranging from 0.74 nm/cycle at 45 W to 1.71 nm/cycle at 90 W. Furthermore, the cyclic process significantly improves surface quality, reducing root‐mean‐square roughness by 8.8% and peak‐to‐valley roughness by 24.3% compared to the as‐deposited film. Surface analysis and density functional theory calculations reveal that the process is enabled by a dynamic synergy between surface oxidation and polymer‐regulated fluorination. Comprehensive characterization results suggest that the cyclic etching process preserves the crystalline structure and chemical purity of the remaining Mo film. This work provides a promising pathway toward precise and tunable Mo etching processes for the next‐generation Mo‐based interconnect architectures.

sources.title: Pre-weakened anodization-assisted rapid thinning of silicon carbide wafers
sources.abstract: Sub-100 µm silicon carbide (SiC) substrates are demanded for thermal management in sub-3 nm architectures, however, the extreme hardness of SiC hinders conventional thinning. Here, we present a hybrid electrochemical-mechanical thinning strategy utilizing a pre-weakened anodization. The anodization was achieved by a designed nonaqueous electrochemical process and then converted the rigid SiC into a carbon-rich porous, stress-dissipating sacrificial layer that absorbs impacts during subsequent conventional diamond wheel grinding. After fine diamond grinding, the bonded pair is separated, yielding ultra-thin (75 µm) SiC wafers that exhibited no visible cracking with reduced XRD peak broadening and a surface roughness of 1.63 nm. In contrast, directly grinding the SiC substrate was not only time-consuming but also consumed four diamond rough-grinding wheels through severe abrasive wear. Moreover, upon removing the protective backside adhesive film after grinding, the thinned wafer immediately warped and fractured. Pre-weakened anodization could effectively reduce fracture during ultrathin SiC wafer fabrication — opening a pathway toward large-diameter wafer processing for advanced packaging applications, including CoWoS and backside power delivery networks.

sources.title: Extreme silicon thinning for back side power delivery network: Si thinning stopping on scaled SiGe etch stop layer
Failure Analysis in Transition: An Industry Survey of Challenges, Priorities, and Standardization Needs in Advanced Packaging and Heterogeneous Integration
sources.abstract: Failure analysis is being reshaped by heterogeneous integration, chiplet-based architectures, hybrid bonding, backside technologies, & increasingly buried package structures. To examine how practitioners view this transition, an anonymous survey was distributed across a broad set of organizations involved in semiconductor design, packaging, systems, tools, & failure analysis. The survey collected approximately one hundred responses & probed organizational background, supported product domains, future priorities in failure analysis, critical bottlenecks, sample preparation challenges, emerging architecture specific pain points, & perceived needs for workflow acceleration & data standardization. The results show that heterogeneous integration, chiplet, and three-dimensional products dominate the respondent base at 69%, while package & heterogeneous integration failure analysis received the highest importance rating at 7.92 out of 10. Hybrid bonding emerged as the most difficult new architecture to analyze at 54%, higher-resolution non-destructive imaging ranked as the most important future accelerator at 8.18 out of 10, and 83% of respondents supported formalized data standardization frameworks. The complete survey data are provided in Appendix A (Table II) to improve transparency & support future benchmarking.

sources.title: Enabling the Angstrom Era: 2D material-based multi-bridge-channel complementary field effect transistors
sources.abstract: This review presents a strategic roadmap for integrating two-dimensional materials (2DMs) into multi-bridge channel (MBC) complementary field-effect transistors (CFETs). It highlights key integration challenges, essential design considerations, and industrialization strategies for 2DM-MBC CFETs. These advances are expected to enable ultra-small, energy-efficient, and high-performance devices in the Angstrom Era that transcend the scaling limitations of silicon technology, paving the way for innovative applications in artificial intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), and edge computing.

sources.title: In-situ Co-Integration of Ru-based Buried Power Rails and nTSVs for Advanced Backside Power Delivery
sources.abstract: ABSTRACT The relentless scaling of semiconductor technology necessitates transformative solutions for power delivery networks (PDNs). Backside PDNs have emerged as a promising approach by decoupling power and signal interconnects. However, the integration of key components like buried power rails (BPRs) and nano-through-silicon vias (nTSVs) faces significant challenges, including interfacial instability and stringent alignment requirements. This work introduces a robust integration strategy utilizing Ruthenium (Ru) as the fill material for both BPRs and nTSVs, leveraging its superior chemical stability. An in-situ co-integration scheme is demonstrated, featuring a self-aligned etching process that enables the precise formation of nTSVs directly onto the BPRs, eliminating critical overlay constraints. An atomic layer deposition process achieves simultaneous, void-free, and conformal Ru metallization without a separate diffusion barrier. Furthermore, an innovative ion-beam thinning-back process is successfully implemented for the precise recess of Ru, overcoming the polishing challenges associated with this hard metal. Electrical characterization reveals an excellent and consistent line resistance of 11.4-11.8 Ω/μm for the co-integrated interconnects. The electromigration performance is rigorously assessed, and a comprehensive multiphysics model is established, showing strong agreement between experimental and simulated failure times, thereby validating its predictive accuracy. This work provides a holistic solution that paves the way for high-performance and highly reliable backside PDNs in advanced 3D integrated circuits (ICs).

sources.title: Unifying Heterogeneous and Monolithic Integration via Dual-sided 3D Technology
sources.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI), has been occupying the central position in recent technological advancement, propelled by exponentially increasing computing resources, which in turn stimulate the demand on higher level 3D integration for integrated circuits. However, current frontside-only integration is inevitably bottlenecked by the routing congestion and parasitic degradation on the wafer frontside, blocking the further down scaling. Fortunately, the underutilized backside space of wafer provides inimitable opportunities to break this blockage. Here, we demonstrate the "Flip 3D" (F3D) technology which utilizes both sides of wafer to capture the ultra-high-density connectivity of monolithic integration while maintaining the architectural flexibility of heterogeneous integration. F3D technology enables the co-integration of logic, memory, and connectivity with significantly reduced interconnect parasitics. Experimentally, F3D technology was verified on a FinFET test vehicle in a dual-sided form, successfully integrating logic, temperature sensors, optical modules, on-chip memory, and high-density computing-in-memory cells. We further introduce "Hyper 3D" (H3D) technology for dual-sided system-on-wafer integration. Our results validate that this unified dual-sided scheme provides effective solution to the "computing," "memory," and "connectivity" walls. This work establishes a scalable roadmap for multi-layer on-chip systems, providing a full-3D hardware strategy for the next generation of AI hardware.

sources.title: Breaking Physics Limits: How 2nm Chip Technology Powers Next-Gen 3D ICs
sources.venue: Fusion of Multidisciplinary Research An International Journal
sources.abstract: The breakthrough 2nm chip technology represents a significant leap in semiconductor innovation, promising enhanced performance and reduced power consumption across multiple industries. While current chip technologies have served us well, the 2nm process is set to deliver a remarkable 12\% boost in energy efficiency, fundamentally transforming how we design and build next-generation electronic devices. This advancement comes at a crucial time, as we witness unprecedented demands in consumer electronics, automotive systems, healthcare devices, and artificial intelligence applications. Additionally, the recent launch of Imec's design pathfinding PDK in February 2024 has opened new possibilities for system research and training. With TSMC's planned production rollout in 2025, we stand at the threshold of a new era in semiconductor manufacturing. In this comprehensive guide, we will explore the intricate details of 2nm chip technology, from its revolutionary architecture to its practical applications in 3D ICs. We will examine how this technology incorporates advanced features like nanosheet devices and backside power grids, ultimately shaping the future of high-performance computing and mobile devices.

sources.title: Focus Session: Advanced CMOS and 5.5D Packaging: Perspectives and Challenges for Design, Reliability and Security
sources.venue: Design, Automation, and Test in Europe
sources.abstract: AI workloads are driving exceptional demand for performance and energy efficiency, forcing semiconductor innovation to advance along two major directions simultaneously. On the device roadmap, the transition from FinFETs to gate-all-around nanosheet FETs and, subsequently, monolithic 3D Complementary FETs (CFETs) is enabling scaling toward the 2 nm era and beyond while targeting aggressive logic density. In parallel, advanced packaging, spanning 2.5D integration on silicon interposers, true 3D stacking, and hybrid 5.5D assemblies, is becoming essential to deliver ultra-high bandwidth, low-energy die-to-die connectivity required by rapidly growing AI model sizes and the resulting memory-wall bottlenecks. This focus session discusses the opportunities and challenges of this co-evolution, with emphasis on system-technology co-optimization and the inevitable need for multiphysics analysis across electrical, thermal, mechanical, and reliability domains. We highlight how reliability and security concerns are increasingly shaping architectural and packaging choices, and we discuss the role of deep learning as a practical enabler for faster simulation and design-space exploration under rising complexity.

findings.claim: Failure analysis and debug are a flagged bottleneck for backside and hybrid-bonded architectures. Backside power delivery networks (BPDNs) add buried structures and block conventional probing access, which complicates fault isolation.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The survey (arXiv preprint, not peer reviewed, about 100 self-selected respondents) lists backside technologies among the architectures reshaping failure analysis. Its most specific difficulty finding is about hybrid bonding, not BSPDN. The inkjet paper says FA resolution is limited by probe needles and wire bonds, and it needed a custom printed redistribution layer to analyse a BSPDN structure with OBIRCH. Together they suggest FA workflows for BSPDN are still being invented, but neither abstract quantifies a BSPDN-specific yield or time-to-diagnosis penalty.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Hybrid bonding emerged as the most difficult new architecture to analyze at 54%

findings.claim: Co-integrating buried power rails (BPRs) and nano-TSVs (nTSVs) is described as difficult, with interfacial instability and tight alignment cited as unresolved challenges. The proposed Ru-based fix is a single-group demonstration.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The abstract itself states the challenges. It reports line resistance of 11.4-11.8 Ω/μm and a multiphysics electromigration model that matches experimental failure times. It reports no yield, no statistical spread across wafers and no scale-up data, and the ion-beam thinning-back step replaces polishing, so its manufacturability at volume is not shown. This is one abstract.
findings.supporting_excerpt: However, the integration of key components like buried power rails (BPRs) and nano-through-silicon vias (nTSVs) faces significant challenges, including interfacial instability and stringent alignment requirements.

findings.claim: Wafer thinning for BPDN is an extra process-risk step. The abstracts show hard-material thinning is slow and wears consumables, and one thinning paper is available only as a title.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The SiC paper reports that the baseline direct grinding was slow and consumed four diamond wheels, so a new hybrid anodization process was needed. SiC is mentioned as a thermal-management substrate for sub-3 nm, and BPDN is named only as a possible application. Ultra-thin (75 µm) SiC is not the same as the silicon thinning used in BPDN. The Si-thinning/SiGe etch-stop paper (src_8744718e19) has no abstract, so only its title shows that stopping on a scaled etch-stop layer is a focus of work. Neither abstract gives thickness-uniformity or yield data for BPDN flows.
findings.supporting_excerpt: directly grinding the SiC substrate was not only time-consuming but also consumed four diamond rough-grinding wheels through severe abrasive wear.

findings.claim: No consensus on the backside and buried power metal is visible. Ru and Mo are both pursued, and each has hard-metal processing problems (polishing for Ru, controlled etching for Mo). This leaves supply-chain and process-maturity risk.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The Ru paper says polishing a hard metal is a challenge and works around it with ion-beam thinning-back. The Mo paper presents a cyclic CHF3/O2 etch for Mo films that lists BPDN among several target applications, alongside interconnects and 3D NAND. It reports blanket-film etch linearity and roughness, not patterned-structure or integration results. Both are early-stage lab results (the Mo paper has 0 citations), so this is an inference about fragmentation, not evidence of failure. The timing is a judgement.

findings.claim: Reliability, thermal and security concerns are described as increasingly shaping architecture and packaging choices. The abstracts provide no BPDN-specific quantification of thermal or reliability penalties, which is an evidence gap.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The DATE focus session (conference abstract) states the need for electrical, thermal, mechanical and reliability analysis in advanced CMOS and 5.5D packaging, and does not mention BPDN in its abstract. The SiC paper notes demand for thermal management in sub-3 nm architectures. Neither shows a measured BPDN heat-removal or electromigration problem. This should be read as an unquantified risk area, not a demonstrated failure.

findings.claim: Dual-sided ('Flip 3D') integration is a possible next step beyond power-only backside use, but it rests on a non-peer-reviewed FinFET test vehicle. It would add complexity and further stretch failure-analysis and process readiness.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The Research Square preprint is not peer reviewed. It claims the scheme solves the 'computing', 'memory' and 'connectivity' walls on the basis of a FinFET test vehicle, and its abstract is truncated. It reports no yield, cost or thermal data. Whether this would displace or merely extend BPDN is unknown. The link to survey-reported FA difficulty is my inference.

findings.claim: Some retrieved papers overstate or loosely report BPDN-adjacent benefits and schedules: a '12% energy efficiency' figure and a 2025 production date are cited without sourcing in the abstract, and a 2D-material CFET roadmap is framed as an expected enabler.
findings.label: unverified_claim
findings.rationale: src_0a3405b8e0 is a general overview with promotional wording ('breakthrough', 'revolutionary'). It does not isolate the contribution of backside power from the 2nm node as a whole, and its 12% figure and TSMC timing are not backed by data in the abstract. src_27b9f0d6ea is a review whose benefits are 'expected', and BPDN is not mentioned in its abstract. Neither is primary evidence for BPDN performance or schedule.

hype_flags: 'Breaking Physics Limits' / 'revolutionary' 2nm framing: promotional wording, a single efficiency figure (12%) not attributed to backside power, and no data in the abstract.
'Provides effective solution to the computing, memory and connectivity walls' (Flip 3D): a broad claim from a FinFET test vehicle in a non-peer-reviewed preprint.
'Expected to enable ultra-small, energy-efficient... devices' (2D-material CFET review): a forward-looking roadmap, not demonstrated BPDN-relevant performance.
'Promising pathway' / 'robust integration strategy' language in the Mo etch and Ru BPR papers: results are lab-scale and report no yield or volume-manufacturing data.

finding.claim: S3 is stated more broadly than its single source supports. The source is one non-peer-reviewed arXiv preprint based only on thermal simulation. S3 extends the finding to "3D/2.5D chiplet packages", but the abstract reports BSPDN penalties for 3D configurations and says only that benefits hold in simplified uniform scenarios. No measured silicon data back it. The finding also gives no magnitude of the penalty.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstract scopes the penalty to 3D configurations and to nanosheet technology. S3's "2.5D" wording and its verified_fact label overstate what a single simulation preprint shows. The result should be read as a model-based warning, not an established effect.
finding.supporting_excerpt: BSPDN configurations in 3D, although beneficial in simplified uniform scenarios, exhibit pronounced thermal penalties under realistic, localized workloads due to limited lateral heat spreading.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S2 says a "recurring" literature finding is that BSPDN increases thermal resistance. Only src_a91300a32b states this, and it is a cooling-proposal paper. The device-level paper src_7762759087 reports that parasitic effects dominate circuit dynamic performance over self-heating. It also finds backside contacts better at suppressing self-heating. src_26b3f5b1fe, as far as its abstract shows, frames backside power as reducing resistance loss and does not claim higher thermal resistance. The evidence is thinner and more mixed than "recurring" implies.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: Citing src_7762759087 and src_26b3f5b1fe in support of S2 overstates agreement. One abstract states the thermal-resistance claim directly. Another ranks self-heating as secondary to parasitics for circuit speed. Self-heating still worsens HCI and BTI, so the thermal risk is real, but its magnitude is not quantified.
finding.supporting_excerpt: parasitic effects dominate circuit dynamic performance compared to self-heating effects (SHEs)
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S10 reports only the negative side of failure analysis. The same chapter reviews EFI methods that remain applicable to BPD ICs: e-beam and atomic force probing, x-ray and magnetic field imaging, and lock-in thermography. The Intel PowerVia abstract also says fault isolation capability is detailed. src_5148be71d2 demonstrates OBIRCH on a BSPDN structure. The finding should be framed as degraded and costly rather than blocked.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The omission of workable methods inflates the severity of the risk. The chapter itself says it assesses each method's potential for improvement, which S10 does not mention.
finding.supporting_excerpt: This chapter provides an overview of EFI methods that are still applicable to ICs with BPD networks, including e-beam and atomic force probing, x-ray and magnetic field imaging, and lock-in thermography.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S4, S5 and S6 rest on two 2026 arXiv preprints that use EDA and simulation only. The backside clock-mesh result comes from OpenROAD with SPICE on GT2N, a 2 nm nanosheet technology the abstract does not describe as production silicon. The CSCO signal-integrity claims come from the framework's own experiments. None of this is silicon-validated or peer-reviewed. "Research has moved beyond power-only BSPDN" is a trend claim drawn from just two papers. The S5 and S6 "verified_fact" labels do not convey that these are simulated, self-reported gains.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstracts report improvements, such as 45% lower skew, on four benchmarks in a research flow. These cannot be generalized to commercial BSPDN nodes. The CSCO abstract asserts "severe" SI degradation as motivation, not as a measured finding. S6 should be treated as a hypothesis and not as an established fact.

finding.claim: S7 cites src_b1bae9c128, which has no abstract and is available as title and metadata only, as support for specific manufacturing constraints. It cannot support them. The thinning and lithography-correction claims are actually backed by src_dbfbe09f9a. The bonding claim is backed by src_f00c9d96cf, which also reports a mitigation: sub-10 nm residual grid distortion with a low-distortion bonding approach. S7 presents the constraints as open problems and leaves out this partial progress.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The metadata-only citation inflates the apparent evidence base. The balance of the finding is also skewed towards unsolved problems, even though the bonding abstract describes an evaluated fix.

finding.claim: S8 says cooling "is being co-designed" with the BSPDN, but both cited sources are proposals backed by finite-element or homogenized numerical modeling. Neither abstract shows fabricated embedded-microchannel BSPDN hardware or measured thermal benefit. Phrased as current practice, this overstates maturity.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: One abstract says "we propose" and describes FEA. The other describes developing a model that "can potentially offer" balanced performance. Both are conceptual and simulation-stage.

finding.claim: S1 is the only measured-silicon performance result in the findings, and it is a single-vendor, self-reported figure. It comes from one E-core on Intel 4 finFET, compared against "a similar design", not a controlled equivalent. It is not GAA technology. S1 does not caveat that the droop and frequency gains are not independently reproduced. Meanwhile most of the cited risk evidence (thermal, clocking, SI) is simulated, so the findings do not weigh measured benefits against modeled penalties.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The number is accurately quoted, but "platform voltage droop" and "similar design" are not defined in the abstract. Applying the gain to other nodes, designs or vendors would be unsupported.
finding.supporting_excerpt: A fabricated E-core with $\gt 90$% cell utilization showed $\gt 30$% platform voltage droop improvement and 6% frequency benefit compared to a similar design without PowerVia.

limitations: The analysis rests on titles, metadata and abstracts only. Two papers (src_93d0a26339, src_8744718e19) had no abstract, and src_6d3f3e6337 is front matter with no content.

Only 12 papers were retrieved, and most are tangential to BPDN (BPDN is named as an application or example). The corpus contains no direct evidence on BPDN cost, yield, IR-drop benefit, thermal penalty or supplier concentration. These are gaps, not evidence that the problems do not exist.
src_93d0a26339 (TSV electrodeposition) does not mention backside power in its metadata, so its relevance is unclear and it was not used for a finding.
Several sources are preprints or not peer reviewed (src_bf3b12f944 on arXiv, src_45682c8d2d on Research Square). Many papers have 0 citations and are recent.
Search coverage is narrow and risk-oriented. Industry roadmaps, foundry disclosures and conference papers (for example IEDM, VLSI) that would quantify BPDN risks may be missing.
Only titles, metadata and abstracts were reviewed. Several abstracts are truncated, and three sources have no abstract.
The evidence set has no TSMC or Samsung BSPDN sources and no independent replication of the Intel PowerVia result, so cross-vendor comparison could not be checked.
Several sources are 2026 preprints or very recent papers with few or no citations. Their reliability could not be assessed beyond what the abstract states.
S11 and the manufacturing-constraint parts of S7 look adequately supported by their abstracts, so they were not challenged beyond the citation issue noted.

sources.abstract: [0000]    Methods, systems, and devices for low resistance structures in systems are described. The described techniques provide for various structures of a power delivery network (PDN), each associated with a reduced resistance relative to other PDN structures. The PDN may include multiple through silicon vias (TSVs) having a relatively small footprint coupled with a metallic pad, where the TSVs may have a relatively small pitch between adjacent ones of the TSVs. In some examples, the PDN structure may include layers between the multiple TSVs and the metallic pad, where each metal layer may be separated by a respective set of vias including various conductive materials. sources.title: Refresh Latency Indication for Refresh Operations [US20260237417A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Apparatuses and techniques for implementing refresh latency indication for refresh operations are described. A memory system may separate memory dies into different ranks. Sending separate refresh commands to each rank congests the command bus. Sending a common refresh command to multiple ranks, on the other hand, causes a large current spike as many dies initiate the refresh operation at the same time. To efficiently prevent the large current spike and thereby lower the costs of a power delivery network, different dies can delay initiation of the refresh commands by different amounts. To do so, a host device can program different dies with different refresh latency indications, which determine lengths of each delay period before starting the refresh operation. The dies can also operate based on an enablement indication that enables the refresh latency mechanism. Staggering the start times of refresh operations can also control current spikes without regard to ranks.

draft.summary: Research on backside power delivery is still growing: OpenAlex works rose from 48 in 2024 to 77 in 2025, and 85 so far in 2026 against 60 at the same date in 2025 (+41.7%). The strongest commercial evidence is Intel's own 10-K, which says Intel 18A introduces backside power (PowerVia) in high-volume manufacturing and will be used across multiple generations of its CPUs [M1, M2, M4]. The only measured-silicon result is a single-vendor, self-reported Intel 4 test showing a >30% voltage droop improvement and a 6% frequency gain [S1, C7]. Most of the evidence on thermal, clocking and signal-integrity penalties is simulation or preprint work, and several earlier findings were challenged as overstated [S2, S3, S4, C1, C2, C4, C6]. Open manufacturing and failure-analysis issues remain [S7, S10, R1, R2, R3, R4]. Patent filings are broad across logic, memory and equipment players [P1, P3, P4], but year-to-date filings are down 17.7% (partly publication lag). Intel's share price has fallen sharply and is highly volatile [T1, T2]. Evidence of external customers, yields, cost and competitor timing is missing, and the X agent did not run.
draft.plain_summary: Backside power delivery moves a chip's power wiring to the underside of the silicon so the top side has more room for signals. Intel says it has started using this in its newest manufacturing process, and research interest keeps growing. The main thing that could hold it back is heat and the difficulty of building and testing chips this way at scale, and most of the heat evidence so far comes from computer simulations rather than real chips.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Intel's 10-K (filed 2026-01-23) states 18A with PowerVia is its high-volume process and will serve multiple generations of client and server CPUs [M1, M2]. Measured benefits come from one Intel 4 test [S1, C7]. The findings contain no yield, shipment volume or external customer data, so the pace of the ramp is unverified. Intel's share price is down 43.3% over one month with very high volatility, which adds timing risk [T1, T2].

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Intel says it is extending backside power into future nodes, pairing it with high-NA EUV for 14A development [M4]. Patent activity from several firms suggests others are pursuing the approach [P1, K4, K5]. The retrieved filings of TSMC, Micron and other companies do not mention the topic, so competitor deployment timing is not shown [M5]. Whether others adopt backside power on a comparable schedule is therefore unsupported by the findings.

horizons.label: forecast

The evidence says little about this horizon beyond Intel's multi-generation intent [M2]. Research activity is not proof of commercial success.

Intel's weak share price shows financial stress that could affect its ability to fund the roadmap [T1, T2]. Benefit claims rest on one self-reported measurement [C7] and some loosely sourced claims [R7].

invalidation_conditions.label: assumption
invalidation_conditions.text: Measured silicon showing that thermal or signal-integrity penalties outweigh power-delivery benefits in production designs [S3, S6, S2].

invalidation_conditions.label: assumption
invalidation_conditions.text: Evidence of poor yield, delay or retreat from backside power on 18A or later Intel nodes [M1, M2, M4].

conflicting_evidence.label: ai_interpretation
conflicting_evidence.text: S1 is the only measured-silicon result: a single-vendor, self-reported figure on one E-core on a finFET node and compared with 'a similar design'. Most risk evidence is simulated, so measured benefits are not weighed against modeled penalties [C7].

conflicting_evidence.label: ai_interpretation
conflicting_evidence.text: The thermal-penalty claim is thinner and more mixed than 'recurring' implies: a device-level paper finds parasitics dominate over self-heating and backside contacts suppress self-heating [S2, S9, C2]. The non-uniform-workload penalty comes from one non-peer-reviewed simulation preprint [S3, C1].

conflicting_evidence.label: ai_interpretation
conflicting_evidence.text: The backside clock-mesh and signal-integrity findings come from two simulation-only 2026 preprints, not silicon [S4, S5, S6, C4].

conflicting_evidence.label: ai_interpretation
conflicting_evidence.text: Patent publications cooled year to date (-17.7%) while research output rose, which sends mixed momentum signals [P1, P4].

themes.name: Enablers and mitigation: wafer thinning, bonding, materials, thermal design and failure analysis

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Equipment and materials suppliers are filing patents on fabrication processes and substrates [P3, K3, K6]. Integration is still described as difficult: buried-power-rail/nTSV co-integration has unresolved interface and alignment issues, and thinning is slow and wears consumables [R2, R3]. Failure analysis is degraded and costly rather than blocked [S10, C3, R1].

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Partial progress exists, such as sub-10 nm residual grid distortion in a low-distortion bonding approach [C5]. No consensus on backside metal (Ru versus Mo) is visible, and each has hard-metal processing problems [R4]. Backside cooling proposals are modeled, not shown in hardware [S8, C6]. The evidence does not show whether these will be solved on a useful timescale.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Thermal modeling of 3D stacks with backside power remains immature (accurate transient simulation including BEOL is open), and dual-sided integration would add complexity [S11, R6]. The cited evidence is silent on commercial outcomes this far out.

bull.label: forecast
bull.narrative: Bonding, thinning and contact processes mature, with partial results already reported [C5], and suppliers' patenting [P3] turns into tooling and materials demand as backside power spreads. Co-designed cooling reaches hardware [S8].

base.label: forecast
base.narrative: Process steps improve incrementally while thermal, thinning and metal-choice questions stay open [R2, R3, R4, S11]. Failure-analysis methods adapt at higher cost [S10, C3].

bear.label: forecast
bear.narrative: Manufacturing integration, thermal management or test costs prove too high and limit adoption outside a few products [R1, R2, R3, S3]. Supplier patents do not become revenue [P3].

catalysts.label: forecast
catalysts.text: Peer-reviewed or silicon-validated demonstrations of nTSV/BPR co-integration, low-distortion bonding or embedded cooling [R2, C5, C6].

catalysts.label: forecast
catalysts.text: Convergence on a backside metal choice [R4].

risks.label: ai_interpretation
risks.text: Several enabling results are single-group demonstrations, preprints or title-only sources with thin evidence [R2, R3, C5].

risks.label: ai_interpretation
risks.text: Failure analysis and debug are flagged bottlenecks, and a dual-sided future would stretch them further [R1, R6, S10].

risks.label: ai_interpretation
risks.text: No BPDN-specific quantification of thermal or reliability penalties exists in the retrieved abstracts [R5].

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation

Caveats: a single-vendor self-reported result [C7], and thermal, signal-integrity, failure-analysis and process-integration issues remain open, largely evidenced by simulation [S2, S3, S6, S10, R2, C1, C2, C4].

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation

The findings contain no yield, shipment, revenue or cost data attributable to backside power, and no other manufacturer is shown in production [M5].

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: The only adoption-like evidence is Intel's plan to use 18A for its own client and server CPUs [M2]. No external customer, design win or purchase evidence is in the findings, so a rating is not supported.

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: Intel is investing across 18A and plans for 14A, with R&D at 26.1% of revenue [M1, M4, K1]. Patent filings come from logic, memory and equipment firms [P1, P3, K4, K5, K6]. Of the companies whose filings were checked, only Intel's mention the topic [M5], and Intel's financial stress shown in its share price is a caveat [T1].

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: Intel claims an industry first in high-volume backside power [M1] and is extending it to later nodes [M4]. TSMC, Micron and others hold related patents [K4, K5], but their filings do not mention it [M5], so competitor timing is unknown. The lead is claimed by Intel itself and not independently verified.

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: Equipment and materials suppliers are patenting enabling processes [P3, K6, K3], but integration issues remain: nTSV/BPR co-integration, slow thinning, no consensus on Ru versus Mo, and bonding distortion with only partial mitigation [R2, R3, R4, C5]. No supplier revenue or capacity evidence is present.

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: Level 3 (elevated). Intel states volume use on 18A [M1, M2], but benefits rest on one self-reported measurement [C7], thermal and failure-analysis issues are unresolved or costly [S2, S3, S10, C1, C2, C3], and the production evidence comes from one company [M5]. Related-stock timing risk adds to this: Intel is down 43.3% over a month with 140.4% annualised volatility [T1, T2]. Not rated higher because a high-volume claim exists and the challenge findings are mostly low to medium severity, and not lower because no customers, yields or competitor production are evidenced.
